extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors to Nature: researchers and specialist scientists (physics, physiology, meteorology, botany, anthropology, optics, ballistics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying evaluative criteria and practical standards from short scientific letters and methods notes (correspondence, technical notes, and presidential address) in a general science journal. Focuses on what counts as acceptable evidence, method, and exposition across multiple disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance of periodogram intensities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use combined probabilities/odds across multiple periodogram intensities to assess the reality of periodicities (example: "the odds that at least nine of the fifteen intensities are not due to luck work out at more than 2000 to 1, while the odds in favour of seven at least are 14,000 to 1").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single high peak; evaluate the joint probability that multiple intensities are not due to chance. Quote combined-odds statements where appropriate and justify claims of "beyond reasonable doubt" by aggregated evidence rather than isolated maxima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on single high intensities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intensity does not occur alone. "Each intensity does not occur alone. Every period, moreover, to which I attach importance rests on more evidence than mere height in my periodogram."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying important periods, require corroborating evidence beyond the mere height of one spectral intensity (e.g., consistency across datasets, harmonics, or other supporting metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting periodicities in synthetic-curve construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing synthetic curves, treat periodicities according to their intensities rather than assuming equal importance: "the periodicities have all been treated as of equal importance; inspection shows that weighting according to the intensities would almost certainly give a better fit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing synthetic reconstructions of cyclical phenomena, apply intensity-based weighting to improve fit and raise correlation coefficients; justify chosen weights and test sensitivity to weighting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of correlation coefficient (do not equate with degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correlation coefficient demonstrates some connexion but is not a direct measure of the degree of connexion: "the correlation co-efficient of 0·38 ... is sufficient to demonstrate some connexion ... but is in no sense to be treated as a measure of the degree of connexion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report correlation coefficients honestly, and do not overinterpret their magnitude as a complete measure of causal or substantive linkage. Use them as indicators while discussing limitations of the synthetic model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limitations and need for further investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit claims when methods are preliminary or data are incomplete: "the synthetic curve as now drawn represents only a first approximation of the roughest possible character ... In many other ways a more accurate determination of the cycles is required ... I have no resources for carrying my own investigations further for the present; I can only hope that others may be better placed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state that preliminary models are approximations, list known deficiencies, and call for further work or resources rather than overstating certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of school botany gardens for observing animal life
rubrics_metrics.description: School botany gardens should be utilised for observation of animal life and seasonal phenomena: examples include nests in trees, frog awakening and tadpole development, life-histories of moths, dragonflies, newts, beetles, water insects, and pupil participation across ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design school botany instruction to include outdoor lessons, mature plantings and ponds, direct observation of animal life cycles, and practical activities (nest-watching, pond studies) suitable for multiple age groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcription system completeness for Russian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a complete transcription system when rendering Russian into English: "Czech transcription has the advantage of being complete."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a transcription scheme that can represent all Russian phonemes unambiguously; completeness is preferable to ad hoc or partial mappings (avoid using a system that cannot render some sounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetic accuracy in transcription (Czech mappings recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcription should reflect Russian sounds accurately: examples given — Russian 'a' corresponds to Czech 'a'; Russian 'y' pronounced like Czech 'w' (oo as in 'hook'); Russian 'x' rendered by Czech 'ch'; soft/hard mutes expressed by a hook; Russian '1' corresponds to Czech 'y'; use Czech 'é' for certain Russian e sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mappings that reduce mispronunciation and preserve phonetic distinctions; provide concrete letter correspondences and use diacritics or hooks where necessary to capture soft/hard distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of diacritical marks in scientific printing
rubrics_metrics.description: The objection to diacritical marks is "relatively small" since most scientific journals already have the necessary type; newspapers may lag behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific publications should use diacritical marks where required for phonetic accuracy; address practical typesetting issues but do not avoid diacritics solely for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of colour vision must explain contradictory empirical facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid theory of vision must account for numerous facts inconsistent with the trichromatic theory and specifically explain phenomena such as the movement of the positive after-image and other empirical observations (author cites his book and subsequent papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or defending a theory, confront and explain experimental anomalies directly (e.g., after-images, luminosity mismatches, invisible region effects) and cite concrete experimental tests that any satisfactory theory must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain movement of the positive after-image
rubrics_metrics.description: Any theory must explain the movement of the positive after-image in the retina (illustrated by tests such as moving the head while eyes are covered or viewing separated windows then moving the head).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms and predictions that reproduce these simple, repeatable after-image behaviors; include experimental protocols that demonstrate the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for anomalies in color-blindness testing
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory should explain how more than 50% of dangerously colour-blind people can pass the wool test and how dichromics may have luminosity curves similar to normals: "How on this theory can the fact that more than fifty per cent. of dangerously colour blind people can pass the wool test be explained ?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address discrepancies between subjective colour-naming tests and other measures (e.g., luminosity curves); reconcile how different testing methods might yield conflicting classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete textbook treatment of the green flash (distinguish two phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and describe both phenomena called the green flash: (1) an after-image due to eye fatigue from red light, and (2) a rarer atmospheric-dispersion 'spectrum flash' (blue/multicoloured); "If this subject should get into elementary text-books ... at least let the account of it be complete."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook entries should present both mechanisms, name them appropriately, describe typical conditions for each, and avoid conflating an ocular after-image with an atmospheric dispersion phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an intense short-duration spark for instantaneous (shadow) photography
rubrics_metrics.description: Instantaneous (shadow) photography of high-speed projectiles is achieved by an electric spark of great intensity and short duration which projects the bullet's shadow onto the plate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exposure systems around a sufficiently intense, brief spark rather than continuous illumination; shadow photography can omit lenses and capture crisp outlines if the spark characteristics are suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger spark with bullet's compressional (sound) wave for supersonic projectiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off the photographing spark controlled by the compressional wave produced by the flight of the bullet so no wires appear on the plate; requirement: bullet speed greater than sound. For slower bullets, use the muzzle blast but then rifle must be stationary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For supersonic projectiles place a diaphragm/trigger near trajectory to convert the crack wave into an electrical trigger; for subsonic cases use muzzle-blast triggering and account for fixed geometry constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid apparatus elements appearing on plates (place trigger outside imaging house)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange apparatus so "no wires or other portions of the apparatus need appear on the plates" by placing photographic apparatus in a light-tight house and locating the trigger outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use remote triggers and thin light barriers (e.g., sheet of paper) to keep the optical field free of apparatus; design housing and trigger placement to prevent unwanted shadows or obstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate spark potential for timing stability and use signal to coordinate firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulate the potential of the spark since "great irregularities in time occur when the apparatus is not operated at the same potential ... The potential regulator ... trips a switch ... turns on a signal light ... as a signal to the rifle operator to fire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a potential regulator across the charging battery and an interlock/signal to coordinate firing only when the proper potential is reached; maintain stable charging conditions to ensure reproducible timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket trigger position with screening to determine unknown bullet speed
rubrics_metrics.description: If bullet speed is unknown, place a piece of paper or wire screen in front of the plate; if punctured when the plate is developed the bullet passed before the spark occurred; move the trigger and repeat until the bullet position when the spark occurs is bracketed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative bracketing with removable thin screens to locate the spark timing relative to bullet travel, then visually fine-tune the trigger position once approximate timing is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two perpendicular light gaps (plan and elevation) for spatial reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide two light gaps, horizontal and vertical, to take plan and elevation photographs of the same bullet; this is particularly useful to investigate unstable projectiles and to construct their actual space position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dual-view imaging to resolve three-dimensional orientation/tumbling; combine the two projections to reconstruct attitude and motion, and use known geometry to interpret wave-front distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive projectile speed and dynamics from conical sound-wave projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The projected compressional waves from nose and base appear with different slopes due to projection distortion; "The true angle of the conical sound wave in air may ... be readily computed, from which the speed of the bullet producing the wave may be determined."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure slopes/angles in the photographic projection and correct for projection geometry to compute true conical angle and hence projectile speed; document geometric assumptions and measurement uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timing devices to study automatic firearms recoil and obtain pressure-time curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute an interrupter trigger by a timing device (e.g., two electromagnets dropping balls) to fire automatic pistols and to allow controlled leads/lags; by changing the height of the timing ball progressively a series of photographs at calculable time intervals can be secured and a pressure-time curve computed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design repeatable mechanical or electronic timing systems to introduce known delays between firing and imaging; use systematic variation of timing to sample recoil stages and compute derived curves such as pressure vs time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define anthropology as a synthetic, evolutionary study of man and his works
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology defined: "the study of the origin and evolution of man and his works" and "the study of man as he occurs at all known times ... body and soul together" — a synthetic, dynamic discipline that surveys all peoples and times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame anthropological research to be synthetic and evolutionary: integrate biological, psychological, cultural, linguistic, and material evidence across timescales; avoid overly narrow focus on single subfields without synthetic integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropological subdivisions and interdisciplinary scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology should include study of man (body and mind: anatomy, physical anthropology, psychology) and his works (material culture, language, social organisation including law and religion) and should interact with historians, geographers, sociologists, economists, and philologists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating anthropological work, check that it situates findings within broader synthetic categories (body/mind/works), acknowledges relevant neighboring disciplines, and uses methods appropriate to the evolutionary/historical questions addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer historical-school methods: trace stages rather than assume independent origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical school "feels it a duty to trace the various stages through which each type of civilisation has passed, rather than to assume that these stages have followed the succession observable elsewhere"; do not assume independent invention without demonstrating impossibility of transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cultural-historical claims, test hypotheses of diffusion vs independent invention; collect historical and environmental evidence before concluding independent origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value but balance study of 'backward' peoples with advanced civilisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Backward peoples remain valuable for methodological development, but anthropologists "should not concentrate so exclusively upon these lowly cultures" and should also study more civilised peoples to apply methods to complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support research programs that include both simpler societies (for methodological clarity) and advanced societies (to test methods at higher complexity); evaluate proposals for appropriate balance and justification.
